title: Tradeoffs: Managed vs Self-hosted Inference - Sales FAQ & Messaging Blueprint
content:
Purpose:
This note is a concise, pragmatic sales & product messaging FAQ to help AE/SEs and growth PMs quickly answer typical buyer questions about building an in-house inference stack (vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM style) vs buying Redwood. It prioritizes operational risks, time-to-value, and cost-trajectory language that resonates with infra/platform buyers.

Intended audience:
- Technical buyers: platform engineers, infra leads
- ML engineering managers evaluating serving options
- GTM: AE/SEs creating one-pagers for discovery calls

TL;DR (1-2 lines):
- Building: attractive on headline cost and control, but carries long tail of engineering maintenance, fragility around kernel/quantization compatibility, and unpredictable ops load as model/traffic changes.
- Buying Redwood: pays for predictable SLOs, turnkey fallbacks, and tooling that compresses time-to-production; unit economics become favorable once you include engineering cost, regression risk, and incident impact.

Core buyer questions and suggested short answers (scripted):
1) Why not just run vLLM / TGI ourselves?
- Short: You can, if you have 6+ months and a dedicated infra team to continuously tune kernels/quantization, maintain batching/caching logic, and handle emergent regressions. Many teams underestimate ongoing maintenance.
- Expanded: Open stacks give control but assume stable workloads and a specialist ops team. In practice kernel regressions, upstream library changes, and model tokenization quirks cause repeated firefighting. Redwood centralizes that operational burden and provides predictable fallbacks and performance SLAs.

2) Cost: headline GPU cost vs Redwood per-token pricing?
- Short: Raw GPU runtime can look cheaper early but misses engineering and amortized ops cost. We recommend running a 12-month TCO that includes SRE time, incident cost, capacity headroom, and performance degradation risk.
- Talking point: For latency-sensitive or multi-region workloads, the management overhead often flips the math in favor of Redwood after 3–9 months.

3) How do you compare on latency and throughput vs TensorRT-LLM?
- Short: For optimized one-off tensors and fixed model/sequence profiles, TensorRT-LLM can achieve excellent throughput/latency. Redwood matches or beats those numbers in real-world mixed workloads by selecting kernels, micro-optimizations, and routing policies automatically.
- Technical nuance: Self-hosted pipelines rely on brittle tuning per model and per sequence-length distribution. Redwood’s runtime dynamically adapts kernel choices and batching based on live traffic patterns.

4) Can customers bring their own quantized models (Q8/Q4/Q3)?
- Short: Yes — Redwood supports a variety of quantized formats and maintains a compatibility matrix. We also provide recommended quantization profiles per workload to balance scalar quality and cost.

5) What about security/compliance for regulated data?
- Short: For regulated workloads Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) mirrors the same control plane and observability while allowing KMS/HSM and audit log integration. Many customers prefer Private rather than DIY to avoid building audit, key rotation, and compliance pipelines themselves.

Unique Redwood positioning bullets (concise):
- Production-first: not just fastest model, but predictable latency, fallback-safe rollouts, and cost controls.
- Unified surface: same API and tooling across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments — reduces application drift between dev and prod.
- Cost-aware planner: recommends batching, caching and quantization settings tied to actual unit economics by model/route.
- Graceful degradation: automated fallbacks to cheaper or cached results under pressure — keeps SLAs intact where DIY systems often fail open or crash.

Key operational risks of self-hosting to call out (stories to tell):
- Kernel and dependency rot: downstream changes in CUDA, cuDNN, or kernel libraries break optimized paths.
- Regression detection gap: silent quality regressions after quantization or kernel swap are common without robust evals tied to production prompts.
- Staffing cliff: specialized infra engineers are expensive and often split across other priorities; single-person critical knowledge creates risk.
- Capacity mismatch: autoscaling for bursty traffic (prefix-heavy) is nontrivial—leads to throttles or overprovisioning.

Objections and rebuttals matrix (for AE/SE use):
- Objection: “We already have GPUs and a SRE team.” Rebuttal: Great — are they focused on inference runtime fragility, model rollouts, and token-level cost analysis? If yes, pilot Redwood in parallel to compare operational load indicators (MTTR, incident count, cost per 1M tokens).
- Objection: “We want full control to modify kernels.” Rebuttal: Redwood Dedicated and Private provide kernel-level tuning hooks and the ability to pin runtime configs; you gain operational layers without reimplementing the orchestration and observability surface.

Battle-tested technical differentiators (how to explain succinctly):
- Dynamic kernel selection: we pick per-request execution kernels based on model shape/sequence length and runtime telemetry to avoid brittle hand-tuning.
- KV-preservation and prefix caching: reduces compute for chat-style workloads—most DIY stacks miss efficient global cache invalidation strategies.
- Continuous evals and rollback: regressions detected via prompt suites trigger automatic rollback policies; that’s rarely built into open stacks.

Sales enablement asks (what AE/SE should ask the buyer):
- What percent of requests are < 64 tokens, 64-512, >512? (sequence profile affects kernel choice and batch viability)
- How bursty is your traffic (p50, p95, p99 requests/min)?
- Do you have an internal eval suite or SLA-bound prompts?
- What compliance controls are mandatory (region, KMS, audit retention)?

Recommended collateral to arm reps (next 30 days):
- One-pager: “Ops risk table — DIY vs Redwood” (short checklist + quick math)
- Interactive TCO spreadsheet: include SRE FTE, incident cost, overprovisioning factor, and latency penalties
- Short demo flow: show latency parity vs vLLM on mixed prompts and then flip to fallback/rollback sequence
- Case vignette: mid-market company who moved from TGI self-hosted to Redwood Dedicated and reduced MTTR by 78% and token cost by 22% in 6 months

Suggested pilot approach (for SALES):
- 4–6 week technical pilot: compare three signals — latency p99, MTTR for incidents, and token unit cost across identical workload. Redwood offers bridging tooling to import request traces for apples-to-apples comparison.

Open questions for product/engineering (to finalize messaging):
- Exact compatibility matrix and supported quant formats to put in public-facing collateral.
- Benchmarks: standardized mixed-workload p50/p95/p99 vs vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM across small/medium/large models.
- Template prompts for continuous evals that we can reuse in sales proofs.

Next steps (owner: Maya):
- Draft the one-pager + TCO sheet (due 2025-02-20).
- Coordinate benchmark runs with Applied ML (Samir) and publish internal brief (target 2025-03-07).

Notes to self (messy brainstorming snippets):
- Consider a hybrid message: "Buy where you need reliability, build where extreme customization is essential." Use for buyers with deep proprietary kernels.
- Capture three real incident anecdotes for AE storytelling — anonymized.
- Add a tiny flowchart: decision path based on team size, compliance needs, and expected traffic shape.

End of brief.
